item.title: La Mona Lisa queda fuera del alcance del público tras cierre de museos París por temor a las protestas
item.description: Los decepcionados turistas asomaban la cabeza el sábado por las puertas cerradas del Louvre y se lamentaban que no podrían ver a la Mona Lisa, en una jornada en que las galerías y los museos de todo París cerraron como medida de precaución ante las nuevas manifestaciones.
item.dc:creator: Sybille de La Hamaide
item.content:encoded: Los decepcionados turistas asomaban la cabeza el sábado por las puertas cerradas del Louvre y se lamentaban que no podrían ver a la Mona Lisa, en una jornada en que las galerías y los museos de todo París cerraron como medida de precaución ante las nuevas manifestaciones. "Cuando llegamos, pensamos que podría haber algún problema, pero no que el museo estuviera cerrado", dijo la italiana Selena Bertoni, de 31 años, frente al Museo de Orsay. Los cierres se produjeron una semana después de que las manifestaciones a nivel nacional por el costo de vida y el deterioro de los servicios públicos degeneraran en algunos de los peores episodios de violencia callejera que ha vivido Francia en años. La violencia y los daños llevaron al Gobierno a imponer toques de queda localizados y a cerrar muchos lugares públicos antes de las manifestaciones previstas para el sábado. El cierre se extendió a gran parte del sector cultural de la capital, incluidos los museos de la Orangerie, el Jeu de Paume y el Picasso, mientras que todo el complejo de los Jardines de las Tullerías, que da al Louvre, quedó acordonado. "Este es el tercer museo al que llegamos y que está cerrado. Deberían habernos avisado", comentó la francesa Heidi Rosar, de 21 años. En el Louvre, las puertas de hierro negro cerradas con llave bloqueaban el acceso a todo el recinto y al jardín. "Queríamos ver al menos la pirámide", comentó Don Nowschuk, un canadiense de 67 años, refiriéndose a la emblemática entrada acristalada del museo. Nowschuk sugirió que las autoridades locales podrían estar exagerando. "Hay tanta seguridad que uno pensaría que sería suficiente para proteger el museo (...) Es un poco extraño ver tantos policías armados por todo París. Estamos acostumbrados a las armas, pero no así". Las restricciones se extendieron al sector de las artes escénicas. La Ópera de París cerró tanto el Palais Garnier como la Ópera de la Bastilla, alegando motivos de seguridad para el personal y el público.

item.title: Trump says he may move White House press corps
item.description: US President Donald Trump confirmed on Saturday he may move the White House press corps to a different location.
item.dc:creator: Jason Lange
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump confirmed on Saturday he may move the White House press corps to a different location. In a social media post, Trump dismissed a report that he planned to remove the White House press room and restore a historic swimming pool on the site, saying he had never "even thought to do such a stupid thing." But he said he could relocate the press corps from its current position in the White House. "I may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location," Trump said in the post. The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Trump had urged then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt in August to move news conferences out of the White House's James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, although the idea was never implemented. According to the report, the president told aides he would rather have an indoor therapy pool that was installed at the site during Franklin D. Roosevelt's administration. The Nixon administration replaced the pool with the press briefing room. Trump has regularly accused US media of unfair reporting about his administration. Last month, Trump briefly banned journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds and said other outlets could face similar restrictions. Free speech advocates have said the move violated First Amendment protections for a free press. The White House reinstated their access after an order from a federal judge who deemed the ban likely unconstitutional, although the Trump administration is still contesting the case.

item.title: Lightning, Mammoth enjoying strong starts to season
item.description: Through a combined 21 games played, the Tampa Bay Lightning and Utah Mammoth are trending in the right direction: upward in their respective divisions.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Through a combined 21 games played, the Tampa Bay Lightning and Utah Mammoth are trending in the right direction: upward in their respective divisions. The two clubs will meet Saturday night in Salt Lake City in the first of two games against each other this season. Entering the Saturday clash, the Mammoth are atop the Central Division, tied with Minnesota with 14 points through 11 games apiece. After Saturday, the Wild will be the next opponent for the Mammoth -- Tuesday in Salt Lake City. Utah is coming off of a 5-3 setback on Thursday against the Kraken in Seattle. The Mammoth got two goals from Logan Cooley and one tally from Vincent Trocheck, as each forward netted on the power play. The Mammoth went 2-for-3 on the man advantage and outshot the Kraken 36-23. Skating with the Florida Panthers, Carolina Hurricanes and New York Rangers for 13 seasons, the 33-year-old Trocheck was acquired from the Rangers over the summer for Sean Durzi, Cole Beaudoin and a 2027 third-round draft pick. "I think the comfortability with each other and getting back into the rhythm of playing the right way has gotten better each game," said the Pittsburgh native, who has three goals, two assists and is 61.4% on faceoffs. "I think how fast we are and how fast we play is tough to play against, especially when teams aren't able to change (lines)." Stopping pucks has been an issue for Utah goaltenders Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa. Vejmelka is the team's No. 1 goalie with a 5-3-0 mark and a 3.04 goals-against average and an .874 save percentage. The 6-foot-6 Cossa is 2-1-0 with a 3.33 GAA and an .820 save rate. Tampa Bay, which is tied for second place in the Atlantic Division, will conclude a three-game road trip on Saturday after a win against the Vegas Golden Knights and a loss to the Colorado Avalanche. A perennial powerhouse, Colorado entered the game three points behind the Mammoth in the Central. However, the Avalanche crafted an early 3-0 lead, received a four-point night from Nathan MacKinnon, and won 6-3 despite Jake Guentzel scoring twice for the Lightning as their three-game winning streak ended. Nikita Kucherov had a three-point showing in a 6-2 win over the Golden Knights to start the trip. He was held off the scoresheet in Denver and ended the night with 1,137 points, tied with former captain Steven Stamkos for tops in Lightning history. Coach Jon Cooper had one word to describe how he understands his complex playmaker. "Experience. Because I've got to experience Kuch," Cooper said. "You treat everyone fairly, don't treat everyone equally. Kuch is somebody that has garnered, you know, you have to let Kuch breathe out there. "Sometimes, people look and think, 'Is he frustrating?' No, you let Kuch be Kuch." After facing Utah on Saturday night, the Lightning will not play again until a home game Thursday against the Winnipeg Jets, who dealt disgruntled goalie Connor Hellebuyck to the New Jersey Devils on Friday. --Field Level Media

item.title: DT Kompany se encuentra estable, pero estará de baja varias semanas: Bayern Munich
item.description: El entrenador del Bayern Munich, Vincent Kompany, permanece hospitalizado y se encuentra estable tras sufrir un desmayo durante el entrenamiento del equipo filial el viernes, pero estará de baja durante varias semanas, dijo el director deportivo del club, Max Eberl.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: El entrenador del Bayern Munich, Vincent Kompany, permanece hospitalizado y se encuentra estable tras sufrir un desmayo durante el entrenamiento del equipo filial el viernes, pero estará de baja durante varias semanas, dijo el director deportivo del club, Max Eberl. El entrenador belga, de 40 años, llevaba varios días luchando contra un virus y se había perdido algunas sesiones de entrenamiento. Eberl afirmó el sábado que el Bayern dará prioridad a su recuperación y esperará al diagnóstico antes de hablar de una posible reincorporación. "Primero tenemos que averiguar de qué se trata y luego discutiremos con calma cuál será el tiempo de recuperación", declaró Eberl a periodistas en Múnich. "No estamos hablando de días, sino de semanas. Todos debemos tenerlo claro". El Bayern aplazó el partido de su equipo filial tras el desmayo de Kompany, pero en ningún momento se planteó solicitar un aplazamiento del partido de la Bundesliga del domingo en Friburgo, explicó Eberl. El segundo entrenador, Aaron Danks, que se hará cargo del equipo contra el Friburgo, afirmó que había hablado con Kompany únicamente para interesarse por su estado de salud. "Le expliqué que no íbamos a hablar de fútbol. Solo se trataba de interesarme por su salud y asegurarme de que se encuentra bien", dijo Danks. "Todas las decisiones futbolísticas están en nuestras manos". El Bayern lidera la Bundesliga con 14 unidades en seis partidos, por delante del Borussia Dortmund por diferencia de goles, mientras que el Friburgo, tercero, se encuentra a un punto.

item.title: Ucrania afirma que Starlink ha vuelto a la normalidad tras una semana de restricciones
item.description: Ucrania afirmó el sábado que el sistema de satélites Starlink y su versión militar, Starshield, volvían a funcionar a altas velocidades tras más de una semana de restricciones que habían entorpecido las operaciones militares y agravado las tensiones con Estados Unidos.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ucrania afirmó el sábado que el sistema de satélites Starlink y su versión militar, Starshield, volvían a funcionar a altas velocidades tras más de una semana de restricciones que habían entorpecido las operaciones militares y agravado las tensiones con Estados Unidos. Los problemas con los sistemas propiedad de SpaceX, la empresa de Elon Musk, se produjeron después de que el presidente Donald Trump anunciara un acuerdo para comprar gasóleo ruso, al tiempo que presionaba a Kiev para que dejara de atacar las refinerías de petróleo de Moscú. Las autoridades ucranianas afirmaron que las restricciones dificultaron la capacidad del ejército para interceptar drones de ataque rusos y obligaron a cancelar algunas operaciones. "Lo más importante hoy es que Starlink y Starshield han reanudado sus operaciones a las velocidades que tenían antes de las restricciones. Las velocidades se sitúan ahora en el nivel que necesitamos", declaró el presidente Volodimir Zelenski en la aplicación Telegram. Según Zelenski, las velocidades comenzaron a volver a la normalidad durante la noche. El Ministerio de Defensa de Ucrania afirmó el sábado que la conexión se mantenía estable a más de 400 km/h. Mientras estaban vigentes las limitaciones, Ucrania experimentó problemas al intentar operar a velocidades superiores a los 160 km/h. Ucrania no depende de estos sistemas para las operaciones con drones de largo alcance en territorio ruso, pero Starlink es vital para las comunicaciones en primera línea y Starshield se utiliza para operaciones militares en los territorios ocupados. Ni Musk ni Washington han reconocido su responsabilidad en la restricción de Starlink o Starshield en Ucrania. Ambos han declarado públicamente que cualquier decisión de este tipo solo podría haberla tomado la otra parte. Reuters informó que la orden de limitar Starshield procedía del interior de la Casa Blanca. Anteriormente, los gobiernos de Estados Unidos habían pedido en varias ocasiones a SpaceX que activara o desactivara Starlink en distintos países, indicaron las fuentes. Trump declaró el viernes que, si los problemas persistían, "lo solucionaría".

item.title: Around 1,200 Palestinians are displaced in Hebron as Israel begins military operation
item.description: About 1,200 Palestinians were displaced as the military began an operation in the West Bank a day after a Palestinian attack killed two Israeli soldiers.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian attack [USN:L1N4690KO TEXT:"killed two Israeli"] soldiers. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday had said the military would launch a large-scale operation after the soldiers were killed when two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at a military checkpoint near the city. The Israeli military said the gunmen were shot dead. They also said the operation in the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods near the military checkpoint at the entrance of Hebron was to search for militants and weapons. In a statement, it also said the military would carry out demolitions. The Palestinian Authority criticised the operation as a "collective punishment". Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, the head of Hebron's municipality, said around 1,300 faced losing their homes in addition to the 1,200 already displaced. He also said the Israeli operations were motivated by parliamentary elections on Tuesday when Netanyahu's right-wing coalition may lose his majority, opinion polls show. "Netanyahu and the radical ministers in his government are trying to win as many votes as possible from the settlers," Al-Jabari said. The non-governmental organisation the Palestinian Prisoners' Club said Israeli forces had arrested around 70 Palestinians on Friday and Saturday. Israeli officials have not commented on any arrests. NETANYAHU'S GOVERNMENT HAS PRESIDED OVER EXPANSION OF SETTLEMENTS Al-Jabari said the military had demolished shops, factories, homes, and roads in Hebron and that the response was disproportionate and unjustified. Residents in Hebron told Reuters that the military expelled many people with no connection to the Palestinian attackers. "We are calling on officials to stand by us because we are not involved in any of this. There are children. We are isolated; we don’t do anything. This is all arbitrary,” said Majdi Nasser, one of those driven from his home. Residents told Reuters they saw Israeli soldiers marking homes with a black X after their Palestinian occupants had been forced to leave. It was not immediately clear what the X mark meant. Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid [USN:L6N44Y077 TEXT:"expansion"] of settlements, deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Across the West Bank, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement. Yousef Mur, a resident of the Palestinian town of Yatta, said the closures meant he was unable to reach Jerusalem with his daughter for her cancer treatment. "The situation is bad, and we are suffering. When we tried to cross, they fired stun grenades towards us, and my girl got scared on the way. They fired stun grenades towards people. The situation is very difficult," Mur said. (This story has been refiled to remove the repeated word 'when' in paragraph 2.)

item.title: Infantino laughs off resignation talk, touts global support as he seeks reelection
item.description: Gianni Infantino finds himself in a position of strength three months after facing calls to resign.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: FIFA president Gianni Infantino laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning in the wake of the failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, pointing to overwhelming support from member associations around the globe. Three months after facing calls to resign after he abandoned the proposal that sought private investment in a new entity controlling commercial rights linked to major FIFA competitions, Infantino now finds himself in a position of strength. His prospects for reelection strengthened on Friday after the [USN:L1N46902J TEXT:"head of Asian football endorsed him"] for a fourth term, with Asian Football confederation (AFC) President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa saying Asia was united behind Infantino. "I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world. I think what is important is that in an organisation like FIFA, there can be different views, different points of view," Infantino told the BBC as he laughed off a question about whether he had considered stepping down. "But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone ... then we need to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority. "I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all African countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world." The AFC had previously joined European body UEFA and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean, in [USN:L6N4470F3 TEXT:"criticising the FFE proposal"]. But a divided CONCACAF and the AFC's U-turn have left [USN:L4N4691GK TEXT:"Europe increasingly isolated"] while exposing the lack of a viable alternative candidate for the FIFA presidency. Infantino is seeking a fourth term until 2031 and potential candidates must submit their nominations by November 18. He apologised at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich last week over the way the FFE proposal was handled but that did not sway [USN:L8N4611Y3 TEXT:"European football associations"] such as Germany and England. However, the 56-year-old Swiss-Italian administrator added: "It's OK to disagree ... but then we need to be able to move on. "There are different points of view. It's not always easy to bring them all under one roof, but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views," Infantino added. "Then it will be up to the FIFA member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want FIFA to be run."

item.title: Rey Jordania ordena responder con "mano de hierro" a atentado contra iglesia que dejó ocho muertos
item.description: El rey Abdalá de Jordania ordenó el sábado a las fuerzas de seguridad que respondieran con "mano de hierro", mientras las autoridades buscaban a los hombres armados que abrieron fuego y mataron a nueve personas e hirieron a otras 40 durante un funeral celebrado en una iglesia.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi
item.content:encoded: El rey Abdalá de Jordania ordenó el sábado a las fuerzas de seguridad que respondieran con "mano de hierro", mientras las autoridades buscaban a los hombres armados que abrieron fuego y mataron a nueve personas e hirieron a otras 40 durante un funeral celebrado en una iglesia. Los agresores dispararon durante varios minutos a plena luz del día el viernes, durante un funeral celebrado en una iglesia ortodoxa griega de la provincia de Karak, en lo que las autoridades jordanas calificaron de acto de terrorismo extremista. No hubo ninguna reivindicación inmediata de la autoría del inusual ataque contra la minoría cristiana de Jordania. Se reforzó la seguridad en centros comerciales, embajadas extranjeras y otros lugares de todo el país, informó la embajada de Estados Unidos en Amán. Un sacerdote describió cómo él y otras personas ordenaron a los asistentes que se tiraran al suelo en la iglesia ortodoxa griega de San Jorge, situada a unos 120 km al suroeste de Amán. "Se apoderó de los presentes una sensación de pánico", declaró Theodoros Soueiss a Reuters. "Los disparos eran indiscriminados y nunca se sabía dónde podría impactar una bala". El rey Abdalá condenó el "despreciable acto terrorista" mientras presidía una reunión del Consejo de Seguridad Nacional y afirmó que no había lugar para la indulgencia cuando se trata de la vida de los jordanos, informó la Casa Real. Este tipo de atentados son muy poco habituales en Jordania, un Estado relativamente estable en Oriente Medio, aunque las autoridades afirman haber desbaratado varios complots islamistas en los últimos años. Las autoridades indicaron que seguían buscando a los autores del atentado y añadieron que era demasiado pronto para determinar si tenían vínculos con grupos conocidos dentro o fuera de Jordania. "Una masacre en todos los sentidos de la palabra", declaró Tarek Ammarin en un hospital donde se atendía a los heridos. Un familiar de Ammarin resultó herido en el atentado. Las imágenes de video de Reuters mostraban a la policía patrullando el sábado frente a la iglesia de Hamoud, a unos 120 km al suroeste de la capital, Amán. "Esto es consecuencia de una ideología terrorista y de un extremismo ciego, y no permitiremos que la sociedad siga por este camino", declaró el primer ministro Jafar Hassan en una publicación en X. Los cristianos constituyen una minoría de la población jordana. El país alberga varios lugares bíblicos que atraen a peregrinos cristianos de todo el mundo.

item.title: Jordan church attack survivor says assailant pointed handgun at him
item.description: Prayer services had just started at a church in Jordan on Friday when Nasser al-Burqan heard what he thought was an exploding air conditioner. Then the blasts kept coming. He soon realised it was gunfire.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi
item.content:encoded: Prayer services had just started at a church in Jordan on Friday when Nasser al-Burqan heard what he thought was an exploding air conditioner. Then the blasts kept coming. He soon realised it was gunfire. Some people ran away. He said others, some bleeding, tried to hide in their place of worship where a funeral for his relative had been taking place. Word spread among those gathered that there were fatalities. When the shooting finally stopped after several minutes, Burqan said he got a good look at the assailants behind what Jordanian authorities described as an act of extremist terrorism that [USN:L1N46A01M TEXT:"killed eight people"]. “When everything finally quietened down, I looked out the window behind me and I saw two — one was masked, the other was not, he was carrying a handgun,” said Burqan, a lawyer. He said one of the attackers, standing about 2 meters away, pointed the handgun at him and opened fire. Some shattered glass left blood on his face. He said he told people who wanted to take him for medical treatment he was fine. SON SHOT IN THE LEG A short while later his son, who also attended the mass, called him to say he had been shot in the leg and was being treated in hospital. The attack at the Greek Orthodox Hamoud church in Karak governorate, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital Amman, shocked the community, part of Jordan’s Christian minority. Such attacks are rare in Jordan, although authorities in the US-allied kingdom say they have repeatedly foiled plots by Islamist militants in recent years. Jordan's King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist". Authorities have said they are still searching for the attackers, adding it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. There has been no immediate claim of responsibility. Security was stepped up at malls, foreign embassies and other locations across Jordan, the US embassy in Amman said on Saturday, as authorities searched for the gunmen who also wounded 40 people.

item.title: With his first smartphone, Lula seeks to catch up to Brazil's online generation
item.description: His choice to finally adopt a foundational artefact of modern life may be a tacit acknowledgment that the 80-year-old president has failed to keep pace with an electorate that spends much of its life online.
item.dc:creator: Luciana Novaes Magalhaes, Oliver Griffin, Lisandra Paraguassu
item.content:encoded: Just days before his 81st birthday, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva this week took ownership of a brand new smartphone, one that former aides said was his first ever. Lula's choice to finally adopt a foundational artefact of modern life may be a tacit acknowledgment that he has failed to keep pace with a Brazilian electorate that now spends much of its life [USN:L1N45Z0NR TEXT:"online"]. That may count against him in Sunday's [USN:L6N45N1A0 TEXT:"presidential runoff"]. "I’m becoming the king of selfies, a real internet user," Lula told supporters at a recent rally in Brasilia, hinting at his renewed efforts to better navigate social media campaigning. Lula’s new technological adventure illustrates a generational shift in Brazilian politics, where a candidate's ability to convert millions of followers across platforms like TikTok, Instagram and WhatsApp into votes can now catapult them to the upper echelons of Brazilian power. During [USN:L1N45L166 TEXT:"congressional elections"] that took place alongside the first round of this month's presidential vote, a number of younger, social media-savvy candidates dominated their races. Running for the right-wing Liberal Party, Nikolas Ferreira, 30, and Lucas Pavanato, 28, both took more than 3 million votes in their respective races, while leftist candidates who were elected with over half a million votes each included Erika Hilton, 33, and Ana Elisa Silva, who is just 21. LULA LEARNS THE ROPES Lula, a former shoeshine boy turned metal worker, trade union leader and global leftist icon, first ran for president in 1989, and is seeking an unprecedented fourth term in office. Standing in his way is right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who is the [USN:L1N466029 TEXT:"son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro"] and surprised pollsters by topping the first-round vote. The 45-year-old senator has been engaging voters directly with his own YouTube channel. Ana Elisa Silva, a law student from Minas Gerais, joined Lula's inner circle to help him better navigate the unfamiliar social media landscape after his disappointing first-round performance. "In my view, digital communication is not a generational privilege," Silva told Reuters. "Age may influence familiarity with certain platforms and formats, but it does not determine the ability to communicate, mobilize, or build a community." For a politician like Lula — who freely admits his distaste for cellphones — the change required some adjustments, Silva said. "His political communication trajectory predates the internet. (It was) forged through his relationships with workers, trade unions, grassroots movements, and massive rallies," she said. "This experience remains important, but it needs to align with changes in how people consume information, especially young people." THE EVOLUTION OF POLITICS The emerging power of so-called "influencer politicians" represents the natural evolution of a phenomenon that started with politicians reaching out to social media figures for campaign support, said Maximo Zaldivar, regional director for Latin America and the Caribbean at the International Foundation for Electoral Systems. "The influencer has their own political capital," Zaldivar said, referring to their amassed followings across social media platforms. "That's what they bring to the table and no politician can compete with that." Among "influencer politicians," Ferreira sits in a league of his own. A staunch Bolsonaro supporter and the son of an evangelical pastor, he boasts nearly 25 million followers on Instagram, equivalent to more than 10% of Brazil's population. Though anyone can jump on social media, success demands commitment and consistent messaging, said Julia Zanatta, 41, an influential conservative lawmaker from southern Brazil with over 1 million followers on Instagram. She secured more than half a million votes in this month's election. “I never thought about whether I'd reach more people or if I'd displease anyone,” she said.

item.title: As winter nears, heating oil emerges as hurdle for Republicans in US Senate races
item.description: It's a top issue in northern states with competitive Senate races as winter approaches.
item.dc:creator: Tim McLaughlin, Nichola Groom, Timothy Gardner, Leah Douglas
item.content:encoded: Eighty-year-old Rick Russman of New Hampshire spent five decades as a Republican. This year, as his state braces for a winter of soaring heating oil costs, he will vote for Democrat Chris Pappas in one of the country's most closely watched Senate races. For Russman, a resident of Kingston, the situation has become so dire that he will rely on a wood stove to help heat his home this winter rather than on heating oil alone. "Fuel that costs more than $6 a gallon is a huge expense," he said. High heating oil prices are a potent issue in northern states that depend on the fuel like Maine, New Hampshire and Alaska, which have competitive Senate races on November 3 that could determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans maintain control of Congress, according to Reuters interviews with 15 voters, candidates and strategists. Democratic candidates have sought to tie the higher costs to Trump's war with Iran, which has disrupted global diesel supplies. The shortage drove prices for diesel, which is similar to heating oil, to a record high above $6.50 a gallon, making groceries and consumer staples more expensive. Reuters was first to report this week that the US Energy Department [USN:L1N46700H TEXT:"released"] heating oil from reserves in the Northeast. When asked about criticism that Trump's policies have led to soaring heating oil costs that could make Republicans vulnerable, the White House pointed to that fuel release, a move an analyst said was unlikely to affect prices. Heating oil prices have climbed above $6 per gallon nationally, up from about $3.50 a year ago, according to the Energy Information Administration. The costs are a headwind for Republicans, said Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine. "The party in power is held responsible for things like that, and it’s so clearly Trump’s fault because of this Iran war." Nearly 80% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame"] Trump policies for higher costs including energy, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll. In New Hampshire, where 43% of residents use heating oil, Pappas said energy dominates voters' concerns as he challenges Republican John Sununu. "Energy costs and heating oil prices are the beginning and end of every conversation I'm having on the campaign trail," Pappas said. Sununu’s campaign did not respond to several requests for comment. ALASKA EVEN HIGHER In Alaska, where roughly 30% of residents rely on heating oil, the issue has surfaced in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola, who has campaigned on lowering energy costs. In remote Alaska communities, fuel is often shipped long distances. Diesel also generates electricity and powers transportation, pushing up the cost of goods and services. In the Yukon River community of St. Mary's, Mayor Sven Paukan said heating fuel has risen to about $10 per gallon, roughly $2 more than last year. "It's pretty difficult to heat homes nowadays," Paukan said. Sullivan said he supports a "temporary pause of American diesel exports," a policy [USN:SPN45A01C TEXT:"Trump has considered"]. A Peltola spokesperson said the Iran war had helped drive up heating fuel, gasoline and grocery costs in Alaska. Sullivan has said he supports the war but that it should end soon, and this week he encouraged Alaska fishermen to apply for a new $8 billion Trump administration [USN:SPN4650BH TEXT:"program"] to offset diesel costs for farmers. Suzanne Downing, former communications director for the Alaska Republican Party, said heating oil is a concern for Republicans. "Many people in Fairbanks ... pay more in the wintertime for their fuel bill than they do for their mortgage," she said. "The Iran war is being blamed for this." MAINE 'DOUBLE WHAMMY' In Maine, where 54% of homes use heating oil, rising fuel costs have featured in the Senate race between Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson. The costs are even higher for fishermen and farmers who use diesel to power their motors and warm homes with oil. "For them, it really is a double whammy," said Mark Brewer, chair of the political science department at the University of Maine. "Folks who probably have the lowest incomes are the ones who are facing the highest energy costs," said Scott Thistle, spokesperson for MaineHousing, the public housing authority, adding older housing stock and mobile homes are costlier to heat. Gerry Cushman, a fifth-generation lobsterman from Port Clyde, said fishermen were already facing fluctuating prices for their catches. But Cushman said he plans to support Collins, the Republican, arguing that her seniority and influence outweigh voters' frustrations. "If you're a senior senator and you're head of (Senate Committee on Appropriations), you can get more done than a freshman senator,” he said. Collins said after initially supporting the war she has voted several times to bring it to an end. She also pushed the US government to speed the release of $38 million for Maine from the $4 billion federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program and urged Trump to tap the heating oil reserve. That's not enough for Maine lobsterman Dave Cousens of South Thomaston, who plans to vote for Jackson. Cousens blamed high energy costs on Trump's Iran war and said he will be forced to forgo a Florida vacation. "He picked a fight with the wrong country, and we're all paying for it."

item.title: Divided over Israel, Detroit Democrats unite on rising costs for midterm elections
item.description: It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present.
item.dc:creator: Heather Schlitz
item.content:encoded: It was her son’s eighth birthday, but Dayna Broadnax could not afford a present. Broadnax, a 42-year-old single mother of four in Detroit, said soaring gas and grocery prices left little money to pay the bills, let alone buy gifts or throw a birthday party. “It’s hard to tell your kids that you don't have the funds right now to buy them a $3 bag of Skittles,” she said while watching her sons practice with a free basketball team at St. Suzanne Community Resource Center. Ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Broadnax’s concerns are widely shared in Detroit. Jewish, Muslim and Black voters interviewed by Reuters often put affordability ahead of disputes over Israel and Gaza, even as many expressed reservations about Democratic US Senate nominee [USN:L1N4420RK TEXT:"Abdul El-Sayed"]. El-Sayed, who could make history as the first Muslim US senator, faces former congressman Mike Rogers in a competitive race that could help determine control of the Senate. A RealClearPolitics average gives El-Sayed a two-point lead – 48% to 46%. Broadnax has yet to decide who to support, saying she will vote for the candidate most focused on lowering costs. She sometimes skips meals so her children can eat and chooses which bills to pay after gas eats up at least $50 of the $150 she makes on a typical day driving for Lyft. “Being a single mom, trying to take care of four boys out here in America now is too hard,” she said. “Whatever candidate whose main focus is affordability – that’s who I’m going with.” But El-Sayed faces resistance from some voters who would ordinarily be inclined to support a Democrat, particularly over Israel. “Both of the candidates have decided that this election is about Abdul,” said Matt Grossmann, a political science professor at Michigan State University. “He needs to win over voters that would normally support the Democratic candidate and are upset with President Trump but might have reservations about him – personal or policy reservations.” El-Sayed’s challenge is not only keeping uneasy Democrats from voting for Rogers, but getting them to vote at all. Some voters told Reuters that opposing Trump made backing Rogers difficult, while concerns about El-Sayed led others to consider sitting out the race. JEWISH VOTERS’ RESERVATIONS Most Jewish voters in Detroit traditionally vote Democratic, but some have deep reservations about El-Sayed over his views on Israel, particularly his response to a March attack on a suburban synagogue. After a man rammed his truck into Temple Israel while more than 100 children were inside, El-Sayed drew backlash when he said “hurt people hurt people" in reference to the attacker. Though El-Sayed later apologized for the comment, he has continued to draw heavy criticism from a community shaken by the attack. Rabbi Aaron Starr of Congregation Shaarey Zedek said some Jewish men now cover their heads with baseball caps instead of yarmulkes because they fear being targeted if identified as Jews. Starr's synagogue spends twice as much on security measures for its sprawling campus following the attack. Starr and a group of Jewish clergy launched a petition calling for the Democratic Party to agree to a set of “non-negotiable” principles, including acknowledging Israel’s right to exist and Jewish sovereignty in Israel. El-Sayed has not signed the petition or communicated with the group, Starr said. He said he would not vote for the Democratic nominee. “He is hyper-focused on Israel and American supporters of the state of Israel and seemed to be placing an awful lot of blame on Israel for America's problems,” Starr said in his study, where “hurt people help people” yard signs leaned against a wall beside shelves of religious texts. El-Sayed briefly campaigned with Hasan Piker, a left-wing streamer who has drawn criticism over comments about Israel and American Jews. The association has troubled some voters, while others remain more focused on the cost of living. “I don't love the fact that he campaigned with Hasan Piker during the primary,” said Alicia Chandler, a 47-year-old Jewish Detroit resident and former supporter of El-Sayed's Democratic primary opponent Haley Stevens. “But it cost me almost $100 to fill my car with gas yesterday.” El-Sayed has repeatedly pledged to protect Jewish people from antisemitism, saying in an August speech after winning the Democratic primary that his commitment to Jewish safety was “the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.” GAZA AND THE POCKETBOOK In 2024, frustration with the Biden-Harris administration’s support for Israel’s war in Gaza drove many Arab American and Muslim voters in Michigan away from the Democratic ticket, with some backing the Republican Trump or third-party candidates and others choosing not to vote. At Shibam Coffee, a Yemeni coffeehouse in the Arab-majority city of Dearborn, volunteers wearing “Abdul for Senate” shirts gathered over cardamom coffee, honeycomb bread and sambusas before heading out to canvass. The cafe is popular with young Arab Americans, many of whom now support El-Sayed. Sumayah Dhalai, a 22-year-old senior at Wayne State University who plans to vote for El-Sayed, liked his policy position opposing funding for the Israeli government but said her fears about finding a job and affording rent and groceries were a bigger factor in deciding who to vote for. “The overwhelming majority of us are very scared about graduating because everybody’s telling us that everything sucks,” Dhalai said. “As much as I want to say I'm out here fighting for world peace, I have to ensure my own ability to succeed before I can then turn to focus on everybody else's.” While parts of Detroit have benefited from new investment, others have not, including the neighborhood housing St. Suzanne Community Resource Center, where the median household income is just $36,525 and roughly half the children live in poverty, according to US Census data. “The financial stress is continual,” said Steve Wasko, the director of the center where Broadnax's sons play basketball. “Being able to pay your rent, afford your light bill, pay your mortgage, or pay to have your furnace working sufficiently – these are the most common requests that come through the door."

item.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
item.description: Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Jacob Bogage
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress. In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks. Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country: TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “[USN:L1N45M10K TEXT:"bad job"]” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low [USN:S0N4310A5 TEXT:"poverty rate"], low [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"unemployment,"] record highs in the [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"stock market"] and cheaper prices for some food items. But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses. Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends. The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people. “Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family." RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory. Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday. Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election. Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa. Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine. TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity. But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues. "I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special." The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens. At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty. Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday. Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them. FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods. But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade. “What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday. Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran. “They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world. TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic. This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton. At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.” “Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said. Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old." Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents. Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton. "Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't." That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

item.title: L'Ukraine dit que Starlink refonctionne normalement
item.description: Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense. Ces systèmes ont été perturbés pendant plus d'une semaine par des restrictions de service qui ont ralenti les connexions et affecté les opérations militaires de l'Ukraine contre la Russie. "Les systèmes de surveillance du ministère de la Défense enregistrent un retour à une vitesse normale de Starlink/Starshield. Nous enregistrons une vitesse supérieure à 400 km/h. La connexion est stable", a dit Evhenii Khmara à des journalistes. Le président Volodimir Zelensky a confirmé que Starlink et Starshield fonctionnaient de nouveau normalement depuis la nuit dernière. "C'est le plus important aujourd'hui", a-t-il sur l'application de messagerie Telegram. Les restrictions à l'utilisation de Starlink, signalées pour la première fois le 14 octobre, ont affaibli les capacités ukrainiennes d'interception des drones russes et perturbé les communications sur la ligne de front, ont dit les responsables ukrainiens. Selon diverses sources, les vitesses de connexion avaient été réduites à 160 km/h voire moins. Les problèmes de l'Ukraine avec le réseau Starlink, propriété de SpaceX, entreprise d'Elon Musk, sont apparus après l'annonce par le président américain Donald Trump d'un accord avec son homologue russe Vladimir Poutine sur la livraison par la Russie de diesel aux Etats-Unis et le blocage de nouvelles sanctions américaines contre Moscou. Donald Trump a simultanément exigé de l'Ukraine l'arrêt de ses bombardements contre les raffineries russes. Ni Elon Musk ni l'exécutif américain n'ont admis être à l'origine de ces restrictions frappant l'Ukraine et tous deux ont publiquement déclaré qu'une telle décision ne pouvait être prise que par l'autre partie. Reuters a rapporté que l'ordre de limiter l'exploitation de Starshield émanait de la Maison blanche.

item.title: Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France
item.description: The interior minister mobilized 70,000 police nationwide, 10,000 more than on October 17, when vandalism and looting raised questions about the government's ability to maintain order.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Yann Tessier, Crispian Balmer
item.content:encoded: Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of [USN:L1N46608H TEXT:"last week's unrest"]. The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high. The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality. The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at a group of around 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed on a cold, rainy evening. In France's second city, Marseille, youths set fire to rubbish bins to block roads, and hurled rocks and bottles at security forces. Police said several stores, including two jewellery shops, were ransacked. Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse. "In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment trouble. PARIS IN LOCKDOWN Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on October 17. Nunez told reporters the violence was less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage. "What changed was anticipation," he said. He also said far-right activists had sought confrontations with leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, opening a potential new front in the disturbances. Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers [USN:L2N46A00I TEXT:"boarding up storefronts"], [USN:L5N46A022 TEXT:"museums closing their doors"] and more than 20 metro stations shut. Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend. "There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris. Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated. "Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans. PROTESTS RIPPLE ACROSS EUROPE The nationwide disorder began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. It swiftly broadened into a wider protest against the government's economic policies and inspired demonstrations in neighbouring countries. On Saturday [USN:L6N46A05C TEXT:"Belgian police"] used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, with protests also taking place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend, [USN:L2N46A02Y TEXT:"and in Albania"]. Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world's richest nations. "Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters. FAR-RIGHT PARTY HOLDS CONGRESS Many demonstrators accused the government of overreacting to last week's turmoil, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants. "We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student. "My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added. The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city. A [USN:L6N4690NC TEXT:"shooting"] west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. "We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

item.title: Starlink in Ukraine back to normal after week of throttling
item.description: A week of restrictions disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.
item.dc:creator: Yuliia Dysa
item.content:encoded: Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version Starshield were now fully functional after over a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US. Problems with Elon Musk's SpaceX-owned systems came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries. Ukrainian officials said the restrictions, which capped operations at speeds of 160 kilometres per hour (kph), hampered the military's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations. "The main thing for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on the Telegram app. According to Zelenskiy, the speeds started returning to normal overnight. Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday the connection remained stable at over 400 kph. Ukraine does not rely on the systems for long-range drone operations on Russian territory, including attacks on refineries. But Starlink remains [USN:L6N4690ON TEXT:"vital"] for frontline communications, and the deployment of Starshield-enabled medium-range attack drones has helped Ukraine gain the upper hand in several areas of the battlefield this year. LIMITATIONS ORDER The restrictions sparked outrage in Ukraine, particularly as they coincided with disruptions to allied warnings about incoming Russian missile attacks. Kyiv later said it continued to receive US intelligence. Neither Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other. Reuters has reported that the [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"order to throttle"] Starshield came from inside the White House. Previously, US administrations had several times [USN:L4N4691IH TEXT:"asked SpaceX"] to turn Starlink on or off in various countries, sources said. On Friday, contradicting his previous statement that the services had been fully restored, Trump said that if problems persisted, he would "[USN:L6N4690ZQ TEXT:"get it straightened out"]".

item.title: Indonesia cuts pipeline gas exports to Singapore by about 9%
item.description: Indonesia cut 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day (mmscfd) from its pipeline natural gas exports to Singapore starting on Saturday to divert supply to the domestic power sector, upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indonesia cut 31 million standard cubic feet of gas per day (mmscfd) from its pipeline natural gas exports to Singapore starting on Saturday to divert supply to the domestic power sector, upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said. Indonesia cut 15 mmscfd from its supply to Singapore from Natuna and another 16 mmscfd of gas from Sumatra, SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto told Reuters on Saturday. Singapore's Energy Market Authority said the total reduction amounts to 17 bbtud over a period of 18 days, which is "less than 2% of our total daily gas demand of more than 1,000 bbtud". "EMA understands that our importers will pursue all relevant recourse in their contracts for the gas supply disruption," the Energy Market Authority spokesperson said Singapore's Energy Market Authority said state gas buyer GasCo is ready to import more LNG at any time and that the country has sufficient energy supplies for national demand Most of Indonesia’s gas exports to Singapore are delivered via pipeline, and the cuts would account for around 9% of that supply “In order to safeguard the reliability of domestic gas supplies for electricity generation, effective today, gas supplies previously destined for Singapore are being redirected for domestic use,” said Djoko The gas is being redirected to meet electricity needs in Batam, Bintan and Sumatra, he said Batam and several cities in Indonesia's Riau Islands province suffered a [USN:L4N46103P TEXT:"blackout"] that lasted 16 hours earlier this month [USN:L6N4680QU TEXT:"Indonesia energy minister"] Bahlil Lahadalia earlier this week said he would prioritise natural resources use for domestic needs, and review contracts to maintain energy security [USN:L4N45T0LE TEXT:"Singapore generates"] up to 95% of its electricity from natural gas

item.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil sites; strikes reported in Aden
item.description: Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said they launched attacks on Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it downed two missiles, as clashes between the two sides intensified. On another front of an escalating conflict reignited by the Iran war , Yemen's Saudi-backed government said the Houthis also fired three ballistic missiles at coast guard sites in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements, though they reported missile debris falling near the site of one of the purported oil targets. It was not immediately clear if any of the reported attacks had hit their targets in the kingdom or had been intercepted. SAUDIS REPORT DEBRIS FROM INTERCEPTED MISSILES Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline. He also said the group targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. The Saudi-led coalition earlier said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Houthis towards Yanbu and Taif. Saudi Civil Defense said debris from intercepted missiles had fallen in the Mecca and Medina regions, home to Islam's holiest sites visited by millions of Muslim pilgrims every year. It said parts of the intercepted missiles fell in Wadi al-Mughammas in Mecca, while debris also fell in areas in Jeddah, Taif and Rabigh. It was not clear if that was linked to the Houthis' reported targeting of Rabigh oil refinery. The renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce that largely halted cross-border attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa. The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran . In Yemen, the Interior Ministry of the internationally recognised government said two of the Houthis' missiles had struck a coast guard headquarters, while a third hit a coast guard building in the Tawahi district. Houthi spokesman Saree said the group's forces had targeted Saudi-backed military gatherings at what he called Al-Nasr camp and a naval military base in Aden, saying Saudi officers were overseeing the mobilisation there. There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on that assertion. Earlier on Saturday, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense briefly issued alerts warning residents of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as in the holy city of Mecca and the kingdom's second-largest city, Jeddah. About 10 minutes later, the agency said the threat had passed. The Houthis warned airlines earlier this month against using Saudi airspace, exempting only the airspace over Mecca and Medina, as they intensified attacks on the kingdom.

item.title: Jordan king orders 'iron fist' response to deadly church attack
item.description: Jordan's King Abdullah ordered security forces on Saturday to respond with an "iron fist" as authorities searched for gunmen who opened fire and killed nine people during a church funeral service.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi
item.content:encoded: Jordan's King Abdullah ordered security forces on Saturday to respond with an "iron fist" as authorities searched for gunmen who opened fire and killed nine people during a church funeral service. The assailants [USN:L6N46A02E TEXT:"fired for several minutes"] in broad daylight at the church in Karak governorate on Friday, and also wounded 40 people in the rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority. Security was stepped up at malls, foreign embassies and other locations across the country, the US embassy in Amman said. 'A SENSE OF PANIC TOOK HOLD' A priest described how he and others ordered people to get to the ground at Saint George's Greek Orthodox church, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman. "A sense of panic took hold among those present," Theodoros Soueiss told Reuters. "The gunfire was indiscriminate, and you never knew where a bullet might land." King Abdullah condemned the "despicable terrorist act" as he chaired a National Security Council meeting and said there was no room for leniency when it comes to the lives of Jordanians, the royal court said. Such attacks are highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities there say they have foiled several Islamist plots in recent years. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack in the kingdom, a major partner with the US in the fight against militant groups. Officials have said it is too early to determine whether the attackers had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. "A massacre, a massacre in every sense of the word," said Tarek Ammarin at a hospital where the wounded were being treated. A relative of Ammarin's was injured in the attack. Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. Jordan has been among the US allies in the Middle East to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February. Bahjat al-Rushda, mayor of Shihan village in Karak, joined a long list of officials condemning what they called an attack by extremist terrorists. "God willing, this country will remain secure," he said.

item.title: North Korea's Kim crosses new bridge into China as trade ties warm
item.description: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties.
item.dc:creator: Joyce Lee, Eduardo Baptista
item.content:encoded: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, Xinhua reported, crossing a newly opened bridge in a symbolic move seen as highlighting Beijing and Pyongyang's push to expand trade ties. Kim was accompanied during his visit by China's fourth-highest-ranked official Wang Huning, who conveyed greetings from President Xi Jinping, the official Xinhua news agency said. Kim arrived in Dandong via the [USN:L6N46004I TEXT:"New Yalu River Bridge"] connecting North Korea and China , a South Korean government official said on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly. The new bridge is expected to help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development. Its official opening this month is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, after two summits between their leaders in the past 13 months. China, which fought alongside North Korea in the 1950-1953 Korean War, remains Pyongyang's main economic and diplomatic backer and accounts for most of its official trade. CHINESE TV SHOWS KIM WALKING ON BRIDGE But North Korea's deepening military ties with Russia since Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine have led analysts to question whether Pyongyang is becoming less reliant on Beijing. Kim's trip nevertheless points to a renewed push by China and North Korea to bolster their economic relationship. South Korea's Yonhap news agency had earlier reported that Kim was expected to return to North Korea after Saturday's visit. Footage from Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed Kim walking on the bridge, lined by people waving flags, towards North Korea. Xinhua said Wang accompanied Kim to a Korean War memorial in Dandong, where the North Korean leader paid tribute to Chinese People's Volunteer Army soldiers who fought alongside North Korea during the three-year conflict. Kim also toured a Dandong [USN:RTV844HDK TEXT:"automobile factory"], it said. NEW YALU RIVER BRIDGE BOOSTS BILATERAL TIES China and North Korea opened the 3 km (2 mile) New Yalu River Bridge, their most significant [USN:L1N46103M TEXT:"land border crossing"], this month after a long delay, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of strained ties and pandemic-related disruptions. "Kim has given his imprimatur to bilateral trade by crossing the New Yalu River Bridge to enter China," said Christopher Green, a Korea specialist at Leiden University in the Netherlands, saying the delayed opening had shown how dysfunctional the relationship had become. During a meeting on Saturday, Wang told Kim that China was ready to use the bridge's opening to expand personnel exchanges and economic and trade cooperation, Xinhua said. A visit by Kim now is consistent with the current phase of closer economic ties and more frequent high-level exchanges between China and North Korea, said Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think-tank in Shenyang. "The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics," Lu said. "With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further." TRUMP WAITS FOR KIM TO ENGAGE Kim's last known visit to China was in September 2025, to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, when he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Xi made a [USN:L1N42G106 TEXT:"state visit"] to North Korea in June. US President Donald Trump has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but US and South Korean officials see [USN:L1N4690EW TEXT:"fading chances"] of him meeting Kim this year, Reuters reported on Friday. China hosts a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum next month in Shenzhen, which Trump is expected to attend.

item.title: How Trump's energy dominance turned into hubris
item.description: It was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer that enabled Trump to pursue foreign-policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career.
item.dc:creator: Ron Bousso
item.content:encoded: When Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025, [USN:L1N3Q1127 TEXT:"“energy dominance”"] was the bedrock of his economic and foreign policy plans. But an unpopular war with Iran and soaring household fuel costs have now made energy policy a major liability for the US president heading into next month’s midterm elections . Ironically, it was the US position as the world's top oil and gas producer, perhaps more than anything else, that enabled Trump to pursue foreign policy goals that may turn out to be the costliest of his political career. In the first two years of Trump’s second term, vast US oil and gas resources emboldened Washington abroad, strengthened its hand in trade disputes and underpinned a broader effort to restore US geopolitical dominance. Yet the Iran war exposed the central weakness in that vision: dominating energy production does not mean controlling energy prices. What began as a pursuit of US energy independence evolved into a doctrine of energy dominance. That is now looking like energy hubris. UNLEASHING AMERICAN ENERGY The foundations of Trump’s strategy were laid long before his return to office last year. The development of cost-effective techniques to tap the country's onshore shale basins transformed the US into the world’s largest producer of natural gas in 2009 and petroleum in 2018. By 2022, it was the leading exporter of liquefied natural gas, giving Washington unprecedented influence over global energy markets. US crude production rose from around 5.5 million barrels per day in 2010 to nearly 14 million bpd today, around a fifth of global supplies, while the country also accounts for more than a quarter of global LNG exports. No single nation has ever occupied such a commanding position in the global energy system. Trump sought to turn that advantage into a governing doctrine. On his first day back in office, he declared a national energy emergency and ordered the government to [USN:S0N3NI004 TEXT:"“unleash American energy”"], prioritising oil, gas, coal and nuclear power while sidelining renewables. Within weeks, he made “energy dominance” official US policy, establishing the National Energy Dominance Council and reviving his familiar “drill, baby, drill” slogan as the purported cure for elevated inflation and economic anxiety. In an October 2025 proclamation, Trump summed up the philosophy as “maximum production, maximum prosperity, and maximum power”. ENERGY POLICY IS FOREIGN POLICY This doctrine extended far beyond domestic energy policy. The administration’s national security strategy, published last December, explicitly linked US influence in the Western Hemisphere to energy dominance, drawing on the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to oppose European political intervention in the region. In a little over a year, the administration wielded US oil and LNG exports in trade negotiations, promoted energy deals as part of efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war , and highlighted Greenland’s resource wealth in a push for greater influence over the [USN:L6N45E05Y TEXT:"Arctic territory"]. The high-water mark for Trump’s energy doctrine arguably came early this year after [USN:L6N3Y407K TEXT:"Washington removed Venezuelan President"] Nicolas Maduro in a swift military operation. The US subsequently [USN:L1N3ZM1KL TEXT:"took control"] of Venezuelan oil exports and revenues, forced through changes to the country’s hydrocarbons legislation that displaced Chinese companies, and secured an unprecedented agreement granting it access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. By February, Trump’s vision of building an economy and foreign policy around abundant fossil fuel resources appeared to be taking root. The US possessed not only more energy than any rival, but also the ability to use that abundance to shape trade, diplomacy and security. Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran in late February put that doctrine to the test. THE IRAN QUAGMIRE The president initially claimed that the joint campaign with Israel against Iran would last only a few weeks. He also repeatedly indicated that vast US oil and gas resources, together with newfound access to Venezuela’s oil wealth, would shield the economy from any resulting spike in energy costs, which he also suggested would be brief. Those assumptions have not aged well. The war launched on February 28 led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global energy supplies used to flow, triggering one of the largest energy disruptions in modern history. Middle Eastern producers cut output and rerouted exports where possible, while major importers across Asia reduced consumption. This caused oil prices to nearly double in the first two months of the conflict, with global benchmark Brent crude peaking at $118 a barrel in March. That was well below the record [USN:L03220220 TEXT:"$145 reached in 2008"], when Iran-related geopolitical tensions, surging Chinese demand and a weakening US dollar drove prices higher. It was also far less than many had feared, largely thanks to reduced Chinese oil imports, ample crude stocks and the surprising adaptability of global markets. But it still represented a severe shock. Moreover, the risk premium from the Iran war is becoming entrenched. Even though crude flows from the Middle East have mostly recovered, Brent is trading around $110. The conflict has also spread across the Middle East, pulling in most of Washington's Gulf allies, most notably the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, which have suffered multiple deadly attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. This has upended the market’s confidence in the security of Middle Eastern crude, unravelled longstanding supply routes and sent [USN:L6N45R160 TEXT:"shipping prices"] skyrocketing. Trump wanted to put his stamp on global energy markets, but this was clearly not what he had in mind. PAIN AT THE PUMP In one respect, the 2026 energy shock has vindicated Trump’s strategy. The war cemented the US position as the world’s top supplier of crude, refined fuels and LNG, delivering enormous profits to domestic producers and exporters and allowing the US to expand its position in the global market. Energy independence certainly offered US consumers some protection against the energy shock, particularly compared with Asian economies, where prices and demand destruction were much more extreme this year. But that protection has been far from ironclad. US gasoline prices at the pump climbed above $4.60 a gallon in May, the highest level since 2022, while [USN:L1N45211Q TEXT:"diesel"] surged to a record $6.50 a gallon in September as global refining capacity was squeezed. Those increases rapidly became a political problem for the White House as cost-of-living concerns moved to the forefront of the campaign ahead of the midterms on November 3. The administration sought to contain the fuel-price spike by pulling almost every available lever, including [USN:L6N44M0V8 TEXT:"easing biofuel blending mandates"] and, most controversially, reaching a [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"diesel supply agreement"] with Russian President Vladimir Putin. This dynamic underscores the difference between commanding supply and controlling prices. Oil, LNG and refined fuels are internationally traded commodities. US producers sell them at prices shaped by global supply and demand. They don’t typically reserve cheap energy for American households. While Trump briefly floated the idea of a [USN:L6N45E0T3 TEXT:"diesel export ban"], officials ultimately rejected it. Even though a ban might have brought down domestic prices initially, it would likely have resulted in higher fuel prices over the medium term due to global market dynamics. ‘ENERGY SECURITY IS NATIONAL SECURITY’ The administration’s assertion last October that “energy security is national security” appears more relevant than ever. The Iran war has shown that cheap and reliable energy is essential for economic growth, whether it powers heavy industry or the data centres underpinning the artificial intelligence race. But the conflict has also changed the meaning of energy security. For countries dependent on imports, particularly [USN:L6N3ZY18D TEXT:"many in Asia"], the shock has revealed the risks of relying heavily on distant suppliers, vulnerable shipping routes and a concentrated global refining system. Their response is likely to be broader diversification: securing more suppliers, expanding domestic fossil fuel production where possible, accelerating renewable power and shifting more transport towards electricity. That will not kick the US off its lofty energy perch, but it will likely weaken the allure of oil and gas for many countries over the coming years. Trump likely felt emboldened to embark on the Iran war — something his predecessors had baulked at — precisely because US energy independence made a Middle East adventure seem less risky than it had when the US was heavily reliant on Gulf oil and gas. But the conflict has, perhaps permanently, undermined Trump’s promise that energy dominance would guarantee low prices and economic security at home. Hubris can be a dangerous thing.
