item.title: Trump foreign policy hits voters in the pocketbook, imperiling Republicans in midterms
item.description: Voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Donald Trump and imperiling Republicans' control of Congress.
item.dc:creator: Matt Spetalnick
item.content:encoded: Foreign policy is rarely the deciding factor in US midterm elections, when economic considerations usually drive voters’ choices. But this time, with Donald Trump’s war against Iran and his sweeping tariff campaign pushing up costs for Americans, a president’s approach to world affairs has itself become a pocketbook issue. As the November 3 elections approach, there are growing signs that voters are drawing that connection directly, creating a major liability for Trump and his fellow Republicans and imperiling their control of Congress. Those include a Reuters/Ipsos poll earlier this month showing some 78% of Americans [USN:L6N45T0W3 TEXT:"blame Trump's policies"] for rising prices that are outpacing their earnings. Not since 2006, when President George W. Bush’s Republicans lost both legislative chambers while he was mired in the unpopular Iraq war, has a US leader’s handling of international events appeared so central to shaping the midterms outcome. The political backlash for Trump could be even bigger, with opinion polls showing that voters feel the economic pain from high gas prices and rising grocery bills in a way that they didn’t two decades ago. “The bottom line is people are experiencing the impact of Trump’s war and other policies,” said Christopher Preble, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington. “Now voters have a chance to register their discontent with how he’s dealing with all this.” POLITICS DRIVING FOREIGN POLICY With Trump’s [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"approval ratings"] touching historic lows, he has left little doubt, despite his public claims to the contrary, that he sees the straight line voters are drawing between his foreign policy and their cost of living. That has prompted some controversial policy moves in the run-up to the elections. Chief among them was Trump’s lifting of sanctions on [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"Russian diesel"] exports aimed at bringing down fuel prices, a step his critics, including some fellow Republicans, say reinforces the impression that he is increasingly siding with Moscow in its war in Ukraine. He has also pressed Kyiv to halt strikes on [USN:L1N46203J TEXT:"Russian refineries"] as he tries to shift the blame for high US gasoline prices despite experts saying the surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the war he launched alongside Israel against Iran nearly eight months ago. At the same time, he has promised not to order any [USN:FWN45U1SW TEXT:"new attack"] on Iran before the midterms, though the US and Israel are widely reported to be preparing for a possible major escalation after the elections. Polls have shown that most voters oppose the war initiated by Trump, who had campaigned on avoiding new foreign interventions. He has insisted Americans should accept temporarily higher gas prices so that he can block Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. Iran says its nuclear program is for civilian purposes. The UN nuclear watchdog and US intelligence community have assessed that Tehran shuttered a nuclear weapons development program in 2003. Some Republican candidates have [USN:L4N45N1R0 TEXT:"distanced themselves"] from Trump on matters ranging from the conflict in the Middle East to the trade war with Canada and his pressure campaign against Ukraine. For its part, Iran has sought to keep oil prices high and hurt Trump in the midterms by deploying new tactics to target ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz and deliberately prolonging the [USN:L8N46515R TEXT:"diplomatic stalemate"], senior Iranian officials have told Reuters. Defending the administration's approach, White House spokesman Matt Middleton said: "President Trump has always been clear about temporary market disruptions as a result of the conflict in Iran, but the contrast between President Trump’s economic record and Democrats’ ruinous alternative is clear." ‘IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID’ Midterm elections historically have been seen as a referendum on the performance of the incumbent in the White House. And in one election after another in recent decades, the conventional wisdom has been that economic concerns - “it’s the economy, stupid,” as the Clinton-era adage goes - dominate voters’ choices. Opinion polls for this year’s midterms, including the Reuters/Ipsos survey, show that while voters rank foreign policy low on their list of priorities, it is clear that most Americans see some of Trump’s signature moves on the world stage, such as the Iran war and tariffs, feeding into their higher costs. Other polls have shown that a majority of Americans have also soured more broadly on Trump’s international approach. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs said its latest nationwide survey “finds that most Americans believe the Trump administration’s foreign policy actions have negatively impacted America’s global standing and hurt national and household economic conditions.” Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has shaken up the rules-based global order that Washington helped create from the ashes of World War Two while his relations with allies have steadily worsened and the [USN:L1N45G0ZJ TEXT:"limits of US power"] have been increasingly exposed, analysts say. LEGISLATIVE BALANCE OF POWER IN PLAY Against this backdrop, Democrats are widely projected to [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"gain control"] of the House of Representatives in the midterms, with the Senate also seen as increasingly in play. For Republicans, losing either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term. But even with a shift in the balance of power on Capitol Hill on November 3, lawmakers will have a hard time reining in Trump’s capacity to pursue foreign policy as he sees fit. Once the ballots are counted, a big question will be whether Trump will feel either restricted or emboldened on the world stage as he enters what is traditionally considered a lame-duck phase - when a president is barred from running again and no longer faces electoral consequences for decisions made. “For many presidents who feel politically constrained (at home), foreign policy is the area where they are able to act with relative freedom,” said Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington. Analysts say Trump's handling of adversaries such as Iran, Russia, China and even Cuba or his approach to allies across the globe could go either way -- or he could simply lose interest and double down on his string of construction projects, such as the White House ballroom.

Reuters reporters set out to define a heat wave and uncovered something far bigger: "heat storms" that now blanket vast stretches of the planet. On this episode of On Assignment, the journalists behind the investigation, Maurice Tamman and Ben Welsh, explain how extreme heat became a constant feature of modern life, and why they needed a new language to describe it. item.title: Fire devastates former Nazi guest house 'Eagle's Nest'
item.description: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday. Around 200 firefighters and emergency workers near Berchtesgaden in Bavaria were battling the flames after the building, known as the Kehlsteinhaus, caught fire on Friday, police said. Built in 1938 as a guest house for Nazi officials and their guests, the building sits in a spectacular Alpine setting above Berchtesgaden. Adolf Hitler used it occasionally, earning it the nickname "Hitler's Tea House". It is separate from his nearby summer residence, the Berghof. Bild newspaper quoted a police spokesperson as saying the building, preserved after World War Two as a historical monument linked to the Nazi era, had been so badly damaged that it "could probably not be saved". Police said earlier they had detained a man near the site but had not yet established the cause of the fire. "Whether the person is linked to the fire is currently the subject of a criminal investigation," Bavarian police said in a statement.

item.title: US accuses government contractor of leaking classified info to girlfriend's Substack
item.description: The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Trotta
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter. The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, 42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information. A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment. “As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement. “That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably,” Eisenberg said. Brinksman held a top secret security clearance while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said. According to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence. The affidavit only identifies the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles she published. "A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads. That quote appears in a September 28 piece published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez. "Over the past year, I’ve published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets before she launched the newsletter. Chávez did not respond to an email message seeking comment. Investigators allege that on at least five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, some at the top secret level. On some of those dates, Chávez published articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA. According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having worked as a US State Department foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement. The State Department declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: Typhoon Champi sweeps past Taiwan, leaving 1 dead, 500 injured
item.description: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday, killing 1 person and injuring more than 500, downing trees and severing power, as it continued to weaken and head north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there.
item.dc:creator: Yimou Lee, Angie Teo, Ann Wang
item.content:encoded: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday, killing 1 person and injuring more than 500, downing trees and severing power, as it continued to weaken and head north towards the Chinese coast though it was not expected to make landfall there. At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi is weakening though still packing gusts of around 126 kph (78 mph) near its centre, according to Taiwan's Central Weather Administration. The storm was about 170 km (106 miles) northeast of Taiwan, having glanced off the island's northeastern coast in Yilan County early on Saturday, the CWA said. The centre of the storm turned south around midnight, hugging the Yilan coastline before making a rare loop offshore and moving away northward. Wind gusts touched 227 kph (141 mph) in some coastal areas, knocking down power lines and sending roof tiles flying. 'MOST TERRIFYING AROUND MIDNIGHT' "It was most terrifying around midnight," said a retired teacher surnamed Lin as he inspected downed banana trees in his garden in Yilan. "It was a sleepless night. I haven't seen anything like this in many years." The storm's forecast track shows it turning north, tracking up the Chinese coast and eventually moving into southern Japan. Taiwan's fire department said the death toll remained at 1, a man swept away by waves from the island of Liuqiu, with 527 injuries during the heavy wind and torrential rain. Taipower said more than 288,000 homes had lost electricity, though most had been reconnected. The transport ministry said 259 flights were cancelled, an improvement from Friday, when the number was almost 1,000. In the capital Taipei, there were downed trees and on-off squally rain showers. Taipei resident Thomas Wang, 70, said the storm felt like something out of the horror film "Poltergeist". "It was quite scary," he said, out running morning errands. Governments in a swathe of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second day of office and school closures on Saturday. Although more common in summer, typhoons can strike in autumn too. China's emergency management ministry sent a team to the eastern province of Zhejiang as Champi approached, warning of strong winds and heavy rain through Sunday. It said it had readied 400 rescue workers and 600 pieces of equipment, while more than 41,000 firefighters were on emergency duty. In Taizhou, a city on Zhejiang's coast, more than 3,800 fishing boats returned to harbour, offshore fish-farm workers were brought ashore and 2,084 island visitors were evacuated, state media reported. Authorities halted 25 offshore construction projects and suspended 18 passenger ferry routes.

item.title: PHP Foundation 'under-funded' with one full-time staff member, director says
item.description: The PHP project is receiving nearly twice as many proposed code changes as a year ago, yet the number of contributors hasn't doubled, Elizabeth Barron said.
item.dc:creator: Toby Sterling
item.content:encoded: The discovery of two serious flaws in PHP this week set off a global scramble to keep websites [USN:L1N468095 TEXT:"safe from hackers, "]showing just how critical the three-decade-old open-source programming language is to the internet. Yet the nonprofit foundation that supports PHP, which may underpin up to 70% of sites globally, operates on a shoestring budget. “We have one full-time staff member (that's me) and 14 mostly part-time contractors,” Executive Director Elizabeth Barron of the PHP Foundation said via email in an interview on Friday. Board members are unpaid volunteers, and funding comes from donations and grants. The foundatio.n works with outside researchers and companies, including OpenAI and cybersecurity firms Wiz and Calif, to investigate security flaws and coordinate fixes, including Wednesday's patches. While Web security company Cloudflare has reported millions of hacking attempts, Barron said the foundation had no evidence hackers were able to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were disclosed, or on sites that have been patched. "We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems,” she said. Artificial intelligence has proved both a help and a burden to the foundation. It helped researchers find the flaws, which had been present for a decade, and Barron said it made programmers more efficient. However, it is also increasing maintainers' workloads. The PHP project is receiving nearly twice as many proposed code changes as a year ago, “yet the number of contributors hasn't doubled,” she said. Reviewing contributions and bug reports requires “a massive amount of human input and experience.” Recent events have shown how heavily companies and governments rely on PHP, Barron said. “Given that reliance, it is clear that PHP is incredibly under-funded.”

item.title: Fear factory
item.description: How filmmakers turn psychological triggers, practical effects and modest budgets into some of Hollywood's most profitable movies
item.dc:creator: Tiana McGee, Anurag Rao, Travis Hartman
item.content:encoded: Before the film, a cinema fills with rows of seats. Choose a rating, put on headphones, and watch a red door with a peephole loom closer. The camera pushes through the peephole into a dark hallway, where something is waiting. Reduce motion R **May contain jump scares PG Click headphones to turn sound on Before every horror film comes a warning. Not about what’s on the screen; about what it might do to you. Choose your experience wisely. Horror is something you experience, not just watch. You sit back, the lights dim, and you plunge into darkness. A feeling of unease starts to settle on you, but you can’t look away. Instead, Horror invites you to look closer. Something looks off. Everything is too quiet. Your body tenses. Your toes curl. You feel like the smallest thing in the room. Your heart is pounding in your chest and then – Just a glimpse and then it’s gone. But you know it’s still there. A creature. An unknown danger. A silent promise waiting to be kept. Fear Factory How filmmakers turn psychological triggers, practical effects and modest budgets into some of Hollywood's most profitable movies By Tiana McGee , Anurag Rao and Travis Hartman Published October 23, 2026 Fear Factory By Tiana McGee , Anurag Rao and Travis Hartman Published Oct. 23, 2026 06:00 AM EDT Horror movies have seen a dramatic rise in both critical acclaim and financial success. The genre has long been one of the safer box-office bets for studios wringing big returns out of modest budgets. Now, in an industry still recovering from the pandemic, that reliability has become a beacon. Because of this dependability, Michelle Martinez, a senior instructor at Arizona State University’s Film and Media Studies program, sees horror as Hollywood’s lifeline. “That’s how we persist,” she said. “Horror film has always been a ‘yes and’ sport. It’s always been low-budget. Nobody took it seriously until now, really.” We're gonna need a bigger box office Horror films are taking up a larger chunk of the domestic box office. In recent years, a single film has dominated each year’s share. This year’s summer blockbuster Obsession made up almost 29% of horror’s overall box office as of July. 5%10%15%20%0201220132014201520162017201820192020202120222023202420252026 Share of total box office The year's #1 horror film All other horror films A gash is cut across the top of the chart and blood falls out of it into fifteen pools, one per year from 2012 to 2026. Pool depth is horror’s share of total domestic box office, rising from 5.9% in 2012 to 18.2% in 2026, on an axis reading 50% at the cut down to zero at the floor. The bright blood at the foot of each pool is that year’s #1 horror film. Note: Data as of July; box office numbers are for the U.S. & Canada Source: Rentrak Horror isn’t just succeeding at the box office; critics are taking notice as well. Sinners , directed by Ryan Coogler, set in Jim Crow-era Mississippi Delta in 1932, received a record 16 Oscar nominations and earned Michael B. Jordan his first Oscar for Best Actor, marking a distinct return for the genre as a critic darling. In the 1970s and 80s, the slasher subgenre dominated the scene after the success of Halloween in 1978. The rise of VHS helped horror movies with limited releases find much-needed permanent homes on video store shelves, giving audiences greater access and opening the door for films to become cult classics. At the 64th Academy Awards in 1992, The Silence of the Lambs became the first and currently only horror film to win Best Picture. However, the 2000s marked a lull for the genre until 2017, when Jordan Peele’s Get Out seemed to announce a shift. All eyes on horror Horror films began to gain critical acclaim in the 1970s with The Exorcist . However, horror film award counts dropped off after 2000, until Get Out sparked a resurgence that continues today. Source: OMDb (Metacritic aggregate), matched against IMDb Horror-tagged titles. So, what does it mean to make art designed to scare people? Nine ways the camera works on you Different camera techniques have long been one of the most effective tools for unsettling audiences. Here are nine common examples: Dolly zoom Dutch angle Bird's eye view Mirrors Close-ups Off-center subjects Camera behind something POV Shaky cam The dolly zoom pulls you into the character’s mindset during tense moments Creative camera placement adds tension and suspense A bird’s eye view offers distance, so you watch the drama unfold A Dutch angle tilts the shot to signal unease POV shots immerse you in the character’s perspective All movies are built on balancing moments of tension with moments of release or relaxation for viewers. In horror movies, this becomes especially important. Moments of peace, even mundane ones, can lure the audience into a false sense of security. A lull can trick you into letting your guard down before the next high-tension moment/scare. With jump scares, there are often moments of silence or softness before the scare. After these moments, a sudden, sharp musical chord or loud sound effect known as the sting typically occurs at the same moment the threat/danger appears. “It might open with some gore just to set the tone or have a little early pre-scare just to prime you,” Martinez said. “So that you’re ready for the bigger build.” Prepare for a SCARE! Each mark below represents a jumpscare. Over the film’s two-hour runtime, it has 11 scares, but they don’t arrive on a schedule. The first arrives 11 minutes in, three cluster in a four-minute burst around the 30-minute mark, the longest calm runs 25 minutes through the second hour, and the final two land 18 seconds apart with 10 minutes of film still to go. Note: whenjumpscare.com rates none of these 11 as major; that is a judgment about how each moment is staged, not a verdict on how frightening the film is. Scare timestamps and severity are its editorial judgment Source: whenjumpscare.com With these moments of tension and release, less is more. In many movies with higher Metacritic ratings or critical acclaim, there are fewer jump scares per hour. The Scaring Horror films, plotted by how often they make you jump. Films with more scares per hour tend to score worse on average. Scores drift down as scare density rises, but the cloud is wide at every density. Oscar winners such as Alien, Jaws and Get Out sit high on the score axis at a range of densities. Note: One dot per film; 695 films with at least one cataloged jumpscare, so scare-free horror is absent. Rate is scares divided by runtime. Correlation only — dense jumpscares are also the house style of low-budget and late-franchise horror, which critics mark down for many reasons at once. Oscar nominees and winners cover all categories, not just the top awards. Source: whenjumpscare.com for scare timestamps, Metacritic for scores, Academy Awards database for nominations Sound amplifies the menace of the movie, seen or unseen. The score, and other sounds that occur outside the world of the story, can be used to manipulate you into feeling tense in moments where you may not even notice it consciously. Sounds that do exist in the world of the film, whispers or floorboards creaking, suggest that something is not as it should be. Lighting, too, is a pivotal choice for making horror work. Shadows and darkness keep things from the audience, letting them imagine the worst. Horror often uses what’s just out of reach to scare and disturb you. Click to turn out the lights The genre works well as a powerful lens for telling larger stories. Horror, like many other art forms, can reflect societal issues, offering a cathartic way to process hardship and trauma across different communities. By transforming real experiences into frightening yet safe scenarios, horror lets us confront hard topics in a controlled environment. Carrie , a movie based on Stephen King’s novel about a bullied high school girl raised by a fanatically religious and abusive mother, is a front-of-mind example for Martinez. The 1974 novel and the Brian De Palma film are often connected to the landmark abortion rights ruling of Roe v. Wade a year earlier, as both express themes of bodily autonomy and the consequences of “the repressing of female power.” Get Out serves as a social commentary on race and Black exploitation. Released in 2017, the film reflects the evolving discussions around race relations and systemic racism at the time. And films like the summer blockbuster Obsession return to questions of autonomy and critique modern dating culture, turning the “Nice Guy” trope on its head. Horror can also give the audience a safe space to work through emotion. Martinez finds that in her classes, it comes up a lot. “If you’re somebody that’s grieving and you go watch a horror film, it helps you push out that wave of grief,” She said. “When you have art that makes you feel […] It helps you reset. And I think for a lot of people, that’s why they really like it. With horror movies making a comeback in a big way, it’s easy to get swept up in the numbers and why they work, but for Martinez, it’s a bit simpler than that. Horror, she says, is a way to break out of the monotony of daily drudgery. “That’s what musicals do. That’s what horror does. It pinches you awake.” Edited by Julia Wolfe, Nick Zieminski

item.title: AI-discovered bugs may soon trigger fresh disruptions, cyber experts say
item.description: We spoke to seven cybersecurity professionals to learn more.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, A.J. Vicens
item.content:encoded: Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost certain to trigger more disruption along the lines of [USN:FWN4661WD TEXT:"the outages that percolated"] across global government websites this week, according to seven cybersecurity professionals who spoke to Reuters. AI helped drive a doubling of the number of digital flaws discovered year-on-year, according to research due to be published in the coming days by VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm. Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the digital infrastructure firm Cloudflare (NET.N) , told Reuters he was aware of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software” and predicted busy months ahead as AI surfaced long-hidden weaknesses in the fabric of the internet. “I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling,” Prince said in an interview on Thursday. The outages that spread across government sites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on Wednesday happened after the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a venerable programming language that powers a huge swath of the internet. Operators have been rushing to fix their software in anticipation of mass exploitation and, because some felt they could not patch before hackers jumped in, a subset simply [USN:L4N46716K TEXT:"yanked their sites offline"] until they could make them safe. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble to fix PHP came during an already busy week in cybersecurity. The week also brought disclosures of vulnerabilities PHP alternative Node.js and streaming program Plex, breaches tied to AI gateway LiteLLM and development platform Railway, and the revelation that the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had used [USN:L6N4680UW TEXT:"an extraordinarily flimsy cryptographic key"] that potentially put users across the internet at risk. “If we just saw four or five things like this, this week, I would expect we’re going to see a lot more,” Garrity said. “I think there’s going to be a lot more fire drills for anything that’s internet exposed.” TIMELINES SHORTENING The codebases that run modern programs are sprawling and mistakes, or “bugs,” that open up potential avenues for exploitation often crop up in unexpected places. Previously, finding bugs required a baseline level of skill, and taking advantage of those bugs to build digital lockpicks – called “exploits” – could be expected to take weeks or months of work by an experienced professional. That would in the past have provided defenders a little breathing room to fix bugs and gently roll out software updates. AI has effectively thrown those assumptions [USN:L6N42I12G TEXT:"out the window"]. Models can find one bug after another by subjecting codebases to round-the-clock scrutiny, and can turn around exploits in hours. Shane Fry, the chief technology officer of Virginia-based RunSafe Security, said the demonstrated performance of AI models over the past few months had effectively laid to rest any doubts over whether they would change the industry. “What's fundamentally, and unquestionably, changing is the timescale for not only finding vulnerabilities, but how quickly adversaries can weaponize them,” Fry said. SCARY MONSTERS While all the experts Reuters spoke to agreed that defenders’ timelines were getting shorter, they were split on whether AI would lead to a hacker free-for-all. Daniel Stenberg, the lead developer of the file transfer tool curl, argued the vulnerabilities found by AI models tended to be exotic bugs that were difficult for rogue actors to take advantage of. Ramy Rahman, a senior principal solutions engineer at cybersecurity company ArmorCode, said “more disclosed vulnerabilities do not automatically mean more successful attacks." There was tentative evidence of that around the PHP vulnerability that drew worldwide concern this week. Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io said that – like Amazon (AMZN.O) and Cloudflare – it had seen aggressive attempts to take advantage of the bug. But the firm’s head of research, Esteban Borges, said that, as of 2 p.m. Eastern Time on Thursday (1800 GMT), the cybercriminals he tracked appeared to have failed to cobble together a working tool to take advantage of it. Prince, of Cloudflare, told Reuters he had seen anecdotal evidence of compromises linked to the PHP vulnerability. The deluge of AI-driven discoveries might rattle the industry, but would be a net positive in the end, he said, comparing it to slaying the monsters in a haunted house. The confrontation might be scary, he said, but leaving the monsters to lurk quietly behind closed doors was far worse. “The reality is, we’re going to get a lot of this stuff cleaned up,” he said.

item.content:encoded: Environ 1.200 Palestiniens déplacés à Hébron par une opération militaire israélienne JÉRUSALEM, 24 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée israélienne a contraint environ 1.200 Palestiniens à quitter leurs foyers à Hébron, en Cisjordanie occupée, a déclaré samedi un responsable palestinien, au lendemain d'une attaque qui a coûté la vie à deux soldats israéliens. Allemagne-Le "nid d'aigle" des nazis en Bavière incendié Le "nid d'aigle", ancienne résidence des dignitaires du régime nazi dans les montagnes bavaroises du sud de l'Allemagne, a pris feu vendredi soir et un suspect a été arrêté, a annoncé la police allemande. Le dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong Un en visite en Chine Le dirigeant de la Corée du Nord Kim Jong Un s'est rendu samedi en Chine en empruntant un pont tout juste ouvert entre les deux pays, a-t-on appris d'un responsable gouvernemental sud-coréen. L'Ukraine dit que Starlink refonctionne normalement Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense. La Russie et l'Ukraine acceptent un cessez-le-feu à Oleshky La Russie et l'Ukraine ont accepté de respecter un cessez-le-feu dans la ville ukrainienne d'Oleshky, occupée par la Russie, afin de permettre l'évacuation des civils pris au piège des combats, a annoncé vendredi la Maison blanche. L'Autriche expulse quatre diplomates russes, Moscou promet de répliquer Le ministère autrichien des Affaires étrangères a annoncé vendredi l'expulsion de quatre diplomates russes basés à Vienne en raison "d'activités incompatibles avec leur statut diplomatique", expression généralement employée pour des faits d'espionnage. La Corée du Sud propose à nouveau de discuter avec la Corée du Nord de la frontière terrestre Le ministère sud-coréen de la Défense a de nouveau proposé vendredi la tenue de pourparlers militaires avec la Corée du Nord, afin de s'accorder sur le tracé exact de la frontière terrestre entre les deux Corées et de réduire le risque d'affrontements accidentels. Le séisme au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés Le séisme de magnitude 7 survenu au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés, a annoncé vendredi le gouvernement local sur les réseaux sociaux. Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde menacées par les feux de forêt Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde, situées sur l'île indonésienne de Sulawesi, sont menacées par la chaleur et la fumée générées par les pires feux de forêt que le pays ait connus depuis plus d'une décennie, ont déclaré des chercheurs. Arabie saoudite: Nouveau report de forums internationaux à 2027 Deux nouveaux forums internationaux prévus en cette fin d'année en Arabie saoudite ont été reportés à 2027 en raison des attaques que lancent les Houthis, rebelles yéménites proches de l'Iran, sur le royaume, a déclaré vendredi l'Autorité générale des statistiques du pays.

item.content:encoded: La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque de Trappes prolongée PARIS, 24 octobre (Reuters) - La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque commise vendredi dans les Yvelines, qui a fait un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fillette de 12 ans, a été prolongée, a annoncé samedi le parquet national antiterroriste (PNAT). Jordan Bardella reconduit à la présidence du Rassemblement national ORLÉANS, Loiret, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Jordan Bardella a été reconduit samedi à la présidence du Rassemblement national, premier parti d'opposition de France, lors d'un congrès à Orléans (Loiret) où des personnalités de gauche ont participé de leur côté à une manifestation hostile à l'extrême droite. Veillée d'armes avant une nouvelle journée de manifestations, le dispositif sécuritaire renforcé La France se préparait vendredi à une nouvelle journée de manifestations à hauts risques samedi, une semaine après les violences et les pillages survenus en marge de défilés pour les conditions d'enseignement détériorées et contre la vie chère, obligeant l'exécutif à un sursaut. Le Pnat saisi après des tirs dans les Yvelines, sur place Macron dénonce un acte terroriste raciste Le président Emmanuel Macron s'est rendu à Trappes, dans les Yvelines, l'une des communes où un homme à bord d'un véhicule a tiré vendredi à l'arme automatique sur la voie publique, faisant un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fille de 12 ans. France: Premier décès lié au virus Shamonda, aucun risque sanitaire à ce jour selon les autorités Un patient est décédé début octobre du virus de Shamonda, une première en France et dans le monde, a annoncé jeudi le gouvernement, ajoutant qu'il n'y avait à ce stade aucun risque sanitaire pour la population générale au vu des connaissances sur ce virus.
